definition: The automated collection of text, images, or other data from websites, commonly used to build large-scale training datasets for foundation models.
details: Web-scraped datasets like Common Crawl provide much of the raw text used to pretrain large language models, though they raise significant questions around data quality, copyright, consent, and the presence of harmful or low-quality content.

explainer.lead: Web scraping for training data is the automated collection of text, images and other data from websites to build large-scale datasets for foundation models. It matters because scraped corpora supply much of the raw text used to pretrain large language models.

tiers.eli5: It is like a robot copying down everything written on millions of web pages so a computer can learn from it later.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers crawl and filter sites at scale, then deduplicate and clean the text before pretraining. The pitfall is treating scraped volume as quality: without filtering, low-quality and harmful content enters the dataset, and copyright and consent questions remain unresolved.
tiers.paperLevel: The practice is automated extraction of web content into corpora; Common Crawl is a prominent source of raw pretraining text. It carries known limits around data quality, copyright, consent and the presence of harmful or low-quality content.

explainer.example: A team downloads a snapshot of Common Crawl, removes boilerplate and duplicates, and uses the remaining text to pretrain a language model.
